title: Inner Child Review Sheet
intro: Only the changes GPT's review and mine both recommend, each in place in the whole guide: two sections in a new order, ten cuts, three small wording changes and three questions. The agreement card by card, with GPT's advice, is here. Everything else on the turn-109 sheet, both of us would leave as it is.

Approve, Reject or Revise each change, and answer the questions in their boxes. Your answers save in this browser as you click. When you're done, press "Save / send", then "Copy my answers", and paste them into the chat from either account.
Nothing in the guide changes until you approve. The two sections read Human in Pangram as they'd read, and the cuts and wording changes get their checks once you approve them.

suggestions.title: Hear the Guard First: your exchange in one piece

edits.before: Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. At some point you can ask that part, "What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?" Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo!
edits.after: Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. At some point you can ask that part, "What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?"

edits.before: A harder voice can seem more fitting for something that's been in your way. I'd still keep it the same. If that voice isn't there in you yet, borrow it from someone who's been safe for you.
edits.after: It might say this will just be one more performance, and you'll fool yourself again. That one can sting, because there could be something to it. Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. "Tell me what you remember, I'm listening." works well here. It puts you into the role of the Nurturer, which alleviates the instinct to argue back. Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo! If you push past it, you might get exactly the performance it was afraid of. Even if you didn't win an Emmy last year, that can look convincing, with the right words and maybe even tears, while nothing underneath feels any safer.

edits.before: That part doesn't have to move out. It's been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one, and I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there's a grown-up here now who could call it off if things got to be too much. It doesn't have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe it would settle for a lighter cover for now, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I'd listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all.
edits.after: A new roommate doesn't win you over with a speech on move-in day (hopefully, right?). The rent just has to keep showing up. Your Protector earns that guard's trust about the same way, mostly out in ordinary life. The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.

suggestions.title: Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff: the danger lines back with the dream line

edits.before: Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, and of course that's exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. I'd assume that what you tell won't be completely confidential, especially if it sounds like something dangerous. Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

reads.text: You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. Just because Mr. Boopaloopa was your name on WhatsApp doesn't guarantee you're anonymous, by the way.

And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

So I’d ask them, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That's a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn't even bother with that, because whatever they tell you today, the law can change tomorrow.

You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

suggestions.title: Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust: the moral after Mr. Rogers

edits.before: You can see the same move in a dramatized scene from the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, "I can't imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father." He doesn't collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what's worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest "genuinely tested" him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he's very proud of both his sons. Then he says, "But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn't have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective." Like the two truths at bedtime, a true complaint and real love don't cancel each other out, so you can take the true part without giving up your love or defending yourself.

suggestions.title: Untangling the Belonging Bargains: ", which is ordinary"

edits.before: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that's kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that's the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like "Boys don't cry." Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

suggestions.title: How to Forgive Without Forgetting: the gold-star aside

edits.before: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can't be put on a schedule (nobody gets a gold star for forgiving fastest). And you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.
